newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN finds "silent disaster" in hungry North Korea.
newsitem.headline: UN finds "silent disaster" in hungry North Korea.

text.p: U.N. relief officials who returned from North Korea said on Wednesday the country was desperately in need of food and reported severe malnutrition among children.

"It's a silent disaster, an incipient famine," said U.N. children's agency representative in Bangkok, Anthony Hewett, who travelled in the secretive communist country last week with the UNICEF resident officer in Pyongyang, Runar Soerensen.
"It's a famine. It's a very severe situation. There are clearly a lot of people affected," he told a news conference.

U.N. and aid officials have been warning for months of a famine in the making in North Korea, which was badly hit by two harvest failures because of heavy rains and flooding in 1995 and 1996 that destroyed roads and housing and crops.
But the United States and South Korea insist large-scale aid can only be debated at four-nation peace talks including China.

The U.N. World Food Programme, which estimates North Korea needs 1.3 million tonnes of food to meet its basic needs in 1997, has appealed for 200,000 tonnes of food worth $96 million, but has received only $38 million to date.

This is in contrast to the speed with which the international community has responded to Saturday's killer quake in Iran which claimed 1,560 lives, for which pledges have been coming in thick and fast according to relief agencies.
"There were people within the epicentre of the quake of Iran within 24 hours. I was staggered by the speed," said Hewlett.

"Here, in North Korea, people hear one thing, they see our photos, then someone else says it's not a problem. Not knowing what to think, they don't do anything. It's the difference between public judgement and public opinion."
"One side says there will have to be peace talks before we give food, the other side says you have to give food before we have peace talks -- back and forth, back and forth."

Hewett said his misssion found no evidence of starvation deaths, cannibalism or military food rampages reported by refugees and travellers coming out of the secretive country, whose isolationist regime admits foreign visitors including those from U.N. agencies only under strict controls.

But he said he found severe malnutrition among children he visited at nurseries, kindergartens and hospitals in southeastern Kangwon province where health staff had reported that 30 percent of the local people were malnourished.
UNICEF said North Korea reported in April that 15.6 percent of some 2.08 million North Korean children below the age of five were suffering from malnutrition.
But a UNICEF survey in Huichon city, north of Pyongyang, found 50 percent of some 8,860 children registered in nurseries and kindergartens were malnourished.
More than 40,000 kindergartens and nurseries in North Korea have been "running on empty for months", said Hewett.

He said North Koreans were getting by only thanks to alternative food supplies. Many people in the countryside were cultivating small plots and eating herbs, locusts, seaweed and fish. The food situation was slightly better in the capital.
